items.title: v3/windows: SetMenu does not redraw the menu bar unless a menubar theme is set

milestone.title: v3.0.0 GA
milestone.description: Wails v3.0.0 General Availability. Track relevant v3 work here. Beta releases are nightly builds and are not planned as separate milestones.

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `WebviewWindow.SetMenu` calls `w32.DrawMenuBar` only when a menubar theme is configured. An application that sets or replaces a menu at runtime without a theme gets a menu bar that Windows has not been told to redraw.

Verified on master at `3465799f2`.

## Where

`v3/pkg/application/webview_window_windows.go`, `windowsWebviewWindow.setMenu` — the whole function is 29 lines and contains exactly one `DrawMenuBar`, inside the theme branch:

```go
	w32.SetMenu(w.hwnd, w.menu.menu)

	// Set menu background if theme is active
	if w.menubarTheme != nil {
		globalApplication.debug("Applying menubar theme in setMenu", ...)
		w.menubarTheme.SetMenuBackground(w.menu.menu)
		w32.DrawMenuBar(w.hwnd)          // <- only reached with a theme
		w32.InvalidateRect(w.hwnd, nil, true)
	} else {
		globalApplication.debug("No menubar theme to apply in setMenu", ...)
	}
```

## Evidence

```
$ git show master:v3/pkg/application/webview_window_windows.go \
    | awk '/func \(w \*windowsWebviewWindow\) setMenu/,/^}$/' | grep -c DrawMenuBar
1
```

...and that single occurrence is on the themed path.

`SetMenu` is documented as taking effect immediately, and does call through to the platform when the window exists, so the omission is user-visible rather than theoretical.

## Why it matters

`DrawMenuBar` is how Windows is told the menu bar changed; without it the bar is not guaranteed to reflect the new menu, and the window's client area is not recalculated. The same call is correctly made elsewhere in the file for other menu operations — this one path just misses it on the untHemed branch.

## Suggested fix

Move `w32.DrawMenuBar(w.hwnd)` out of the theme branch so it runs after every `SetMenu`, leaving `SetMenuBackground` and `InvalidateRect` where they are.

## Notes

Found while reviewing the Windows menu code for other work. Related: the same function leaks the replaced menu's handles (#6102) and panics on a nil menu — filed separately.

items.title: v3/windows: SetMenu leaks the replaced menu's HMENU and bitmaps

milestone.title: v3.0.0 GA
milestone.description: Wails v3.0.0 General Availability. Track relevant v3 work here. Beta releases are nightly builds and are not planned as separate milestones.

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows, calling `WebviewWindow.SetMenu` on a window that already has a menu discards the previous `*Win32Menu` without destroying its `HMENU` or releasing its bitmaps. Every call leaks, and it is reachable from public API.

Verified on master at `3465799f2`.

## Where

`v3/pkg/application/webview_window_windows.go`, `windowsWebviewWindow.setMenu`:

```go
func (w *windowsWebviewWindow) setMenu(menu *Menu) {
	if w.parent.options.Windows.DisableMenu {
		return
	}
	menu.Update()
	w.menu = NewApplicationMenu(w, menu)   // <- previous w.menu dropped on the floor
	w.menu.parentWindow = w
	w32.SetMenu(w.hwnd, w.menu.menu)
	...
```

## Why `Win32Menu.Update()` does not cover this

`Update()` is careful, and does free what it owns — it builds a new `HMENU`, then on success releases the old bitmaps and destroys the old handle:

```go
	oldDetachedSubmenus.destroyAll()
	if oldHMENU != 0 {
		releaseMenuBitmaps(oldBitmaps, oldMapping)
		w32.DestroyMenu(oldHMENU)
	}
```

But that only frees the previous `HMENU` **of the same `Win32Menu`**. `setMenu` constructs an entirely new `Win32Menu` via `NewApplicationMenu`, so the old object — its `hMenu`, its `bitmaps`, and its `detachedSubmenus` — is never reached by that path and never freed.

## Evidence

`DestroyMenu` is used 13 times across the menu implementation, and zero times in the file that replaces menus:

```
$ for f in webview_window_windows.go menu_windows.go menuitem_windows.go popupmenu_windows.go; do
    printf "%-24s DestroyMenu:%s\n" "$f" "$(git show master:v3/pkg/application/$f | grep -c DestroyMenu)"
  done
webview_window_windows.go DestroyMenu:0
menu_windows.go          DestroyMenu:5
menuitem_windows.go      DestroyMenu:1
popupmenu_windows.go     DestroyMenu:7
```

So the cleanup machinery exists and is used elsewhere; this one path simply does not call it.

## Reachability

`WebviewWindow.SetMenu` is public and applies immediately when the window exists:

```go
func (w *WebviewWindow) SetMenu(menu *Menu) {
	...
	if w.impl != nil {
		InvokeSync(func() {
			w.impl.setMenu(menu)
		})
	}
}
```

`w.menu` is already populated during window creation (`webview_window_windows.go` lines 120, 455, 461), so even the *first* runtime `SetMenu` leaks, and an application that swaps menus in response to state changes leaks on every swap.

## Suggested fix

Free the outgoing menu before replacing it — a `Destroy()` on `Win32Menu` that destroys `hMenu`, releases `bitmaps` and calls `detachedSubmenus.destroyAll()`, called from `setMenu` when `w.menu != nil`.

## Notes

Found while giving the Windows menu code a second pair of eyes for other work; not a regression, and as far as I can tell it has always behaved this way. Related: the same function does not redraw the menu bar unless a menubar theme is set, and panics on a nil menu — filed separately.

items.title: [v3] Default signal handler is constructed but never started — SIGINT/SIGTERM bypass App.Quit and all shutdown hooks

milestone.title: v3.0.0 GA
milestone.description: Wails v3.0.0 General Availability. Track relevant v3 work here. Beta releases are nightly builds and are not planned as separate milestones.

items.body:
## Description

In v3.0.0-beta.19, the default application signal handler is constructed but never started, so SIGINT/SIGTERM do not go through `App.Quit()` — the OS default disposition kills the process immediately and none of the app's cleanup runs (service `ServiceShutdown`, window/tray teardown, `PostShutdown`, etc.).

`pkg/application/signal_handler_desktop.go` builds the handler:

```go
func (a *App) setupSignalHandler(options Options) {
	if !options.DisableDefaultSignalHandler {
		a.signalHandler = signal.NewSignalHandler(a.Quit)
		a.signalHandler.Logger = a.Logger
		a.signalHandler.ExitMessage = func(sig os.Signal) string {
			return "Quitting application..."
		}
	}
}
```

…but nothing ever calls `a.signalHandler.Start()`. `internal/signal.SignalHandler` only registers its `signal.Notify` channel inside `Start()`:

```go
func (s *SignalHandler) Start() { ... }
```

The only `Start()` caller in the whole module is the dev watcher (`internal/commands/watcher.go:67`), not `pkg/application`. So `DisableDefaultSignalHandler` currently has no observable effect: handler or no handler, signals bypass the app.

## Impact

Any v3 app that manages external resources leaks them on Ctrl-C / SIGTERM. In our case (an app that supervises a Docker container and spawned media-player processes), SIGTERM left the container running and the child processes orphaned; the same happens when `wails3 dev` sends its interrupt.

## To Reproduce

1. `wails3 init -t vanilla`, add a `ServiceShutdown` (or `PostShutdown`) that logs/touches a file.
2. `go run .` (or run the built binary), then send SIGTERM (or Ctrl-C).
3. The process dies immediately; the shutdown hook never runs. Expected: "Quitting application..." message and a graceful `App.Quit()`.

## Workaround

```go
app := application.New(application.Options{
	DisableDefaultSignalHandler: true,
	// ...
})
go func() {
	ch := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
	signal.Notify(ch, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	<-ch
	go app.Quit()
	<-ch // second signal: force exit
	os.Exit(1)
}()
```

## Suggested fix

Call `a.signalHandler.Start()` during `App.Run()` (guarded by `DisableDefaultSignalHandler`). Happy to send a PR if that's the preferred shape.

## System

- Wails v3.0.0-beta.19
- Verified on macOS 26 (arm64), Go 1.27; the construct-but-never-start path is platform-independent (`//go:build !ios`).

items.title: [v3] Bound non-chunked runtime HTTP request bodies before buffering

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: New issue awaiting first maintainer look

items.body:
## Problem

The ordinary (non-chunked) v3 runtime HTTP path buffers the entire request body without a byte limit before parsing or validating the runtime call. A reachable deployment without an outer request-size limit can allocate memory proportional to attacker-controlled request size, creating a potential availability risk.

## Affected scope

Reviewed master at `61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111`. The primary concern is server-mode deployments exposing `/wails/runtime` without limiting middleware or a reverse proxy. Application-supplied limits can mitigate exposure. No memory-exhaustion or end-to-end denial-of-service test was run.

## Evidence

- [handleRuntimeRequest](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/transport_http.go#L167-L190) uses `io.Copy(buf, r.Body)` into a growing `bytes.Buffer` before `processBody`.
- The `maxPooledBufferSize` guard only controls buffer retention after the request, not allocation while reading.
- The [chunked path](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/transport_http.go#L193-L215) separately applies `http.MaxBytesReader`; this protection is bypassed by an ordinary request without the chunk header.
- [Server setup](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/application_server.go#L107-L119) configures timeouts, which do not establish a byte ceiling; [routing](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/application_server.go#L205-L235) passes requests through the asset server. No blanket body cap was found in the inspected default wiring.

## Validation approach

Use an isolated server-mode example and a bounded test payload just above the chosen maximum. Exercise a normal `/wails/runtime` request without chunk headers and verify rejection before full buffering. Also test application middleware and reverse-proxy limits. A deliberate OOM test is unnecessary.

## Expected behavior / acceptance criteria

- Apply a documented, optionally configurable byte limit before buffering ordinary runtime bodies.
- Return a consistent oversized-request error (preferably HTTP 413) without dispatching a runtime call.
- Cover below-limit, at-limit and over-limit requests, including bodies without a declared Content-Length.
- Keep supported large-payload/chunked workflows working and document their separate limits.
- Verify that oversized buffers are neither allocated in full nor retained in the pool.

## Related work

#5369 introduced chunked uploads. Its [security review](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5369#discussion_r3205955771) identified memory-exhaustion risks, and [follow-up](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5369#issuecomment-4415496642) added per-chunk and assembled-body limits. Those changes protect the chunked path; this report concerns the ordinary path.

Found during Ripwire structural security triage followed by focused source inspection. Deployment exposure and final severity remain to be validated.

items.title: [v3] Harden built-in MCP null-origin and authentication policy

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: New issue awaiting first maintainer look

items.body:
## Problem

The optional built-in v3 application MCP server accepts `Origin: null` while returning wildcard CORS headers. This permits opaque browser origins through the origin check on an endpoint exposing application-control tools, including caller-supplied JavaScript execution. The observed policy is confirmed; a full browser-to-application exploit has not been demonstrated.

## Affected scope

Reviewed master at `61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111`. Applies only to applications built with the `mcp` tag. The listener defaults to `127.0.0.1:9099`; `WAILS_MCP_HOST` can expose it on another interface. Builds without the tag are unaffected. This concerns the built-in application MCP server, not the separate `wails3 mcp` project-management server.

## Evidence

- [mcpOriginAllowed](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_protocol_enabled.go#L64-L76) explicitly returns true for `Origin: null`.
- [CORS headers and handler](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_protocol_enabled.go#L78-L118) use `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and accept OPTIONS/POST after that check.
- [Tool dispatch](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_protocol_enabled.go#L173-L264) reaches the selected handler without an authentication check in this path.
- [`js_eval`](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_tools_enabled.go#L229-L247) accepts the caller's JavaScript; [eval](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_eval_enabled.go#L49-L75) places it into a script passed to `window.ExecJS`.
- [Existing origin tests](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/61838b39c6749e6b7d019fe4deb646f7641cf111/v3/pkg/application/mcp_enabled_test.go#L200-L222) explicitly expect null origins to be accepted.

A local Go test using the exact extracted origin/CORS functions confirmed: null allowed; ordinary untrusted HTTPS origin denied; localhost allowed; wildcard CORS returned. An opaque-origin browser context is the candidate bypass to validate. Browser local-network restrictions and actual deployment exposure may affect exploitability; no OS command execution or end-to-end browser exploit is claimed.

## Expected behavior / acceptance criteria

- Reject opaque/null origins on privileged MCP requests and preflights unless a deliberate, documented authenticated design requires them.
- Define and enforce the authentication and allowed-origin policy for application-control tools, including non-loopback binds.
- Add regression tests for null, foreign, missing and approved origins; document the intended treatment of non-browser clients.
- Validate the policy with a real browser and an MCP-enabled example app, while preserving supported MCP clients.

## Related work

- #5682 introduced the application MCP server.
- #5896 secures the separate project-management MCP server.
- #6036 addresses related origin/rebinding risks in v2 dev IPC, not this endpoint.

Found during Ripwire structural security triage followed by focused source inspection. Final exploitability and severity remain to be validated.

items.title: [v3/windows] Cannot combine per-pixel transparency and click-through for overlay windows (WebView2)

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Unscheduled feature work beyond GA. Placement here is not a commitment to a specific release. Goose should move items to a numbered milestone only when that release scope is justified.

items.body:
### Wails version family

v3

### Exact Wails version

v3.0.0-alpha2.117

### Operating System

Windows

### Description

On Windows, a frameless always-on-top transparent Wails window cannot do two things at the same time.

1. Empty areas stay see-through. The app below stays visible.
2. Mouse clicks in empty areas reach the app below.

With the current WebView2 setup on Windows, you get one behavior or the other.

**Path A — transparent background (Wails default for frameless transparent)**

- See-through pixels work.
- The window still gets mouse clicks.
- WebView2 child windows (`Chrome_WidgetWin_*`) get the clicks first.
- `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` on the main window is not enough.

**Path B — `IgnoreMouseEvents: true`**

- Clicks pass through to the app below.
- The window becomes a solid white sheet.
- Wails calls `SetLayeredWindowAttributes(hwnd, 0, 255, LWA_ALPHA)` on resize and bounds changes.
- That call breaks per-pixel transparency in WebView2.

Related issues: #4408, #4871, #5229 / PR #4814.

### To Reproduce

1. Create a v3 app with a frameless always-on-top window:

```go
application.WebviewWindowOptions{
    Frameless:                  true,
    AlwaysOnTop:                true,
    BackgroundType:             application.BackgroundTypeTransparent,
    BackgroundColour:           application.NewRGBA(0, 0, 0, 0),
    DefaultContextMenuDisabled: true,
    // Size to monitor via SetPhysicalBounds — not Win32/HTML fullscreen
}
```

2. Load a page with `background: transparent` and visible UI elements.
3. Open another app below the overlay.
4. For Path A, keep `IgnoreMouseEvents: false`. The overlay stays transparent. Clicks do not pass through.
5. For Path B, set `IgnoreMouseEvents: true`. Clicks pass through. The overlay becomes a white sheet.

### Expected behaviour

Both behaviors must work at the same time.

- Transparent WebView2 content over the app below
- Mouse clicks in empty areas reach the app below

### Screenshots

_No response_

### Attempted Fixes

| Approach | Transparency | Click-through |
|----------|-------------|---------------|
| `IgnoreMouseEvents: true` | opaque white | yes |
| `WS_EX_NOREDIRECTIONBITMAP` on host only | yes | no |
| `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` on host + all child windows | yes | no |
| `WebView2CompositionHosting: true` + `UseVisualHosting: true` | yes | no |
| Chromium flag `--disable-direct-composition` | mixed | no |
| Subclass `Chrome_WidgetWin_*` → `WM_NCHITTEST` → `HTTRANSPARENT` | yes | no (partial: no menu / text selection) |
| `EnableWindow(false)` on WebView2 child windows | yes | no (same partial result) |
| `LWA_COLORKEY` chroma key | solid color | partial |
| Toggle `WS_EX_LAYERED` off/on after Wails resize | no | no |

Best result so far uses Path A and disables WebView2 child windows. Context menus stop. Double-click text selection stops. Clicks still do not reach the app below.

WebView2 child windows get mouse input before the main window can pass clicks through. Microsoft documents `CoreWebView2CompositionController` for transparent overlays. Wails sends mouse input into WebView2. It does not pass input to windows below.

We searched #4408, #4871, and #5229. None give a supported way to get both behaviors on a full-screen overlay.

We can provide a minimal repro repo on request.

### System Details

```shell
# Wails
Wails CLI | v3.0.0-alpha2.117

# System
| Name              | Windows 10 Pro                                      |
| Version           | 2009 (Build: 26200)                                 |
| ID                | 25H2                                                |
| Branding          | Windows 11 Pro                                      |
| Platform          | windows                                             |
| Architecture      | amd64                                               |
| Go WebView2Loader | true                                                |
| WebView2 Version  | 150.0.4078.83                                       |
| CPU               | AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D 8-Core Processor                |
| Go Version        | go1.26.5                                            |
```

### Additional context

We build a desktop overlay above a full-screen app at native monitor size. This is a common broadcast or tooling HUD pattern.

An older Electron app got both transparency and click-through. It used `transparent: true`, `setIgnoreMouseEvents(true)`, and `--disable-direct-composition`. We have not found the same working setup in Wails v3 on Windows.

We need documented steps that work, or a built-in overlay mode for transparent click-through windows.

items.title: Fix/Workaround for silent crash when using OpenDirectoryDialog on Windows
items.body:
### Wails version family

v2

### Exact Wails version

v2.15.0

### Operating System

Windows

### Description

I recently encountered a fatal silent crash on Windows when using `runtime.OpenDirectoryDialog` in Wails v2 without a `DefaultDirectory` configured.

When calling `OpenDirectoryDialog` for the very first time without providing a `DefaultDirectory`, the dialog opens successfully, but Windows attempts to save an invalid or empty state to the Windows Explorer Dialog Registry history (`HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\CIDOpen` / `ComDlg32`). 

When you restart the app and trigger the dialog again, Windows attempts to restore this corrupt view state from the registry into the new process. This instantly causes a fatal memory access violation in the COM thread, bringing down the whole Wails application without any stack trace or panic output in the terminal.


### To Reproduce

1. On a fresh Windows installation or with a clean dialog registry history, call `runtime.OpenDirectoryDialog()` without providing a `DefaultDirectory` in the options.
2. Select a directory and completely close the Wails application.
3. Restart the Wails application.
4. Call `runtime.OpenDirectoryDialog()` again. 
5. The application instantly closes/crashes before the dialog is rendered.


### Expected behaviour

The dialog should open successfully on subsequent runs. Wails should either automatically set a safe fallback path internally if `DefaultDirectory` is empty, or properly handle the corrupt registry read so that it doesn't crash the entire host process.


### Screenshots

_No response_

### Attempted Fixes

- Providing a `DefaultDirectory` (e.g. `C:\`) AFTER the crash has already occurred does NOT fix the issue, because Windows still tries to read the corrupt history state first.
- The ONLY way to fix it is to:
  1. Manually delete the cached registry keys (`ComDlg32`, `CIDOpen`, `CIDSave` under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\`) to clear the corrupt state.
  2. Ensure the code ALWAYS provides a valid `DefaultDirectory` from the very first run onward to prevent the corrupt state from being written again.


### System Details


items.body: ### Wails version family v3 ### Exact Wails version v3.0.0-alpha.96 ### Operating System macOS ### Description When double-clicking the application window title bar to trigger the default macOS window resize animation (transitioning from Size A to Size B), the webview content does not continuously resize along with the window frame. Instead, the web content remains static at its initial size throughout the ~1-second animation, and only jumps to the target size once the animation completely finishes. This latency causes a significant visual artifact during the window transition: Empty/blank areas appear between the web content boundaries and the animating window borders. When using a macOS native look with backdrop-filter (blur/translucency（Backdrop: application.MacBackdropTranslucent,）), this lag creates a severe visual rupture—the solid white content background stays fixed while the translucent window frame expands around it. After researching this issue, this behavior appears to be an inherent mechanism of macOS's WKWebView during window "Live Resize" animations, where the WebKit render loop fails to keep frame-level sync with the system WindowServer animation thread. While manually overriding the window resize logic via custom state management or manual JS/Go animation handles could serve as a potential workaround, it introduces significant architectural complexity and state-management overhead. Unless absolutely necessary, I prefer to avoid implementing heavy manual animation hooks. I am curious if there are lighter framework-level solutions, native WKWebView layer configurations (e.g., layer stretch/preserves content flags), or better best practices to smooth out this rendering lag without completely taking over system window management. ### To Reproduce 1.Create a Wails application on macOS with a translucent window background: ``` go Mac: application.MacWindow{ Backdrop: application.MacBackdropTranslucent, } ``` 2.Build a simple web page with a solid background color (e.g., #FFFFFF or #FF0000) so that content boundaries are clearly visible. 3.Launch the app on macOS. 4.Double-click the window title bar (or press Option + click on the green window zoom button) to trigger the system window resize animation. 5.Observe the webview rendering behavior during the ~1-second animation transition. ### Expected behaviour Expected Result: The web content scales continuously and synchronously with the translucent window frame throughout the animation. Actual Result: The web content stays frozen at its initial size, leaving blank/translucent frame gaps during the transition, and abruptly snaps to the target size only after the animation completes. ### Screenshots ### Attempted Fixes Attempted Workaround & Technical Observations I attempted to poll and monitor the window size on the Go backend using a high-frequency ticker (every ~30ms) to notify the frontend of real-time dimension updates: ``` go go func() { for { time.Sleep(30 * time.Millisecond) w, h := window.Size() fmt.Printf("Window size changed to: %d x %d\n", w, h) } }() ``` Observation: During the macOS title bar double-click zoom animation, window.Size() does not emit intermediate size updates frame-by-frame while the transition is playing. Instead, the backend thread remains unaware of any size changes throughout the animation and only receives the final target dimensions (Size B) in a single burst once the animation completely finishes. This confirms that system-level "Live Resize" animations freeze intermediate polling updates at the API level, making backend-driven layout synchronization infeasible. ### System Details ```shell % wails3 doctor Wails (v3.0.0-alpha.96) Wails Doctor # System ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ | Name | MacOS | | Version | 15.7.9 | | ID | 24G830 | | Branding | Sequoia | | Platform | darwin | | Architecture | amd64 | | Apple Silicon | unknown | | CPU | Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8257U CPU @ 1.40GHz | | CPU | Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8257U CPU @ 1.40GHz | | GPU | cores, Metal Support: Metal 3 | | Memory | 16 GB | └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ # Build Environment ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ | Wails CLI | v3.0.0-alpha.96 | | Go Version | go1.26.2 | | -buildmode | exe | | -compiler | gc | | CGO_CFLAGS | | | CGO_CPPFLAGS | | | CGO_CXXFLAGS | | | CGO_ENABLED | 1 | | CGO_LDFLAGS | | | DefaultGODEBUG | cryptocustomrand=1,tlssecpmlkem=0,urlstrictcolons=0 | | GOAMD64 | v1 | | GOARCH | amd64 | | GOOS | darwin | └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ # Dependencies ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ | *NSIS | Not Installed. Install with `brew install makensis`. | | Xcode cli tools | 2410 | | npm | 11.12.1 | | docker | *Docker version 29.4.0, build 9d7ad9f (daemon not running) | | | └────────────────────────── * - Optional Dependency ───────────────────────────┘ # Checking for issues SUCCESS No issues found # Diagnosis SUCCESS Your system is ready for Wails development! items.title: v2.14.0: multipart/form-data request body SIGSEGVs the Linux asset server (webkit2_41) and arrives empty on macOS
items.body:
### Description

Sending a `multipart/form-data` request body from the webview to a handler
mounted as `assetserver.Options{Handler: …}` behaves differently on each
platform in Wails v2.14.0:

- **Linux** (`-tags webkit2_41`, WebKitGTK 4.1): the process dies with `SIGSEGV`
  inside `webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body`.
- **macOS** (WKWebView): the request reaches the handler with the right
  `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=…`, but the body is empty —
  `r.MultipartReader()` gives `NextPart: EOF` after 0 bytes.
- **Windows** (WebView2): works correctly.

The same handler and the same payload sent as a raw `application/octet-stream`
or `text/plain` body arrive whole on all three platforms, at both 32 bytes and
2 MiB — so this is about the *shape* of the body rather than its size.

We hit this while measuring which asset-server transport primitives we could
build on. Linux desktop is not a target for us, so it isn't blocking our work;
we're reporting it because the crash takes the whole process down and seemed
worth having on record. Thanks for Wails — the rest of the asset server behaved
exactly as documented.

### Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| Wails | v2.14.0 |
| Go | 1.27.1 (`runtime.Version()` in the built binary) |
| Linux | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-1022-azure, x86_64 (GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest`) |
| Linux WebKitGTK | `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0` / `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev` `2.52.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.1` |
| Linux build | `wails build -clean -skipbindings -tags webkit2_41` |
| Linux run | under `xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 1280x1024x24"` + `dbus-run-session`, with `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1` and `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1` |
| macOS | macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), arm64; `wails build -clean -skipbindings` |
| Windows (works) | Windows Server 2025 10.0.26100.33296, AMD64; WebView2 / Chromium 151 |

### To reproduce

The excerpts below are taken from our probe rig. It lives in a private
repository, so the relevant parts are inlined here rather than linked.

Mount an ordinary `http.Handler` as the asset server's `Handler`:

```go
err = wails.Run(&options.App{
    Title:  "transport spike",
    Width:  900,
    Height: 700,
    AssetServer: &assetserver.Options{
        Assets:  frontend, // embed.FS sub-FS holding index.html
        Handler: mux,
    },
})
```

Give the mux a handler that reads the request body as multipart:

```go
mux.HandleFunc("/probe/multipart", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    res := map[string]any{
        "method":         r.Method,
        "content_type":   r.Header.Get("Content-Type"),
        "content_length": r.Header.Get("Content-Length"),
    }
    mr, err := r.MultipartReader()
    if err != nil {
        res["parse_error"] = "MultipartReader: " + err.Error()
    } else {
        n := 0
        for {
            part, err := mr.NextPart()
            if err == io.EOF {
                break
            }
            if err != nil {
                res["parse_error"] = "NextPart: " + err.Error()
                break
            }
            b, _ := io.ReadAll(part)
            n += len(b)
        }
        res["bytes"] = n
    }
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(res)
})
```

From the page loaded in the webview, POST a `FormData` body. This 32-byte
version is enough — the payload size makes no difference:

```js
const fd = new FormData();
fd.append('file', new Blob([new Uint8Array(32)]), 'small.bin');
const r = await fetch('/probe/multipart?tag=small', { method: 'POST', body: fd });
const j = await r.json();
```

A ~2 MiB version behaves identically (crash on Linux, 0 bytes on macOS):

```js
const bytes = new Uint8Array(2 * 1024 * 1024);
const fd = new FormData();
fd.append('note', 'spike');
fd.append('file', new Blob([bytes], { type: 'application/octet-stream' }), 'payload.bin');
await fetch('/probe/multipart?tag=main', { method: 'POST', body: fd });
```

### Linux: stack trace

Verbatim from the CI log of the run that first surfaced it:

```
SIGSEGV: segmentation violation
PC=0x7fe561b53e5e m=8 sigcode=1 addr=0x28
signal arrived during cgo execution

goroutine 25 gp=0x2469f42b54a0 m=8 mp=0x2469f4296808 [syscall]:
runtime.cgocall(0x8f6ab0, 0x2469f427bcb8)
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.27.1.linux-amd64/src/runtime/cgocall.go:167 +0x4b fp=0x2469f427bc90 sp=0x2469f427bc58 pc=0x49154b
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver/webview._Cfunc_webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body(0x29d83430)
	_cgo_gotypes.go:437 +0x45 fp=0x2469f427bcb8 sp=0x2469f427bc90 pc=0x817685
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver/webview.webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body.func1(...)
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/webview/webkit2_40+.go:24
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver/webview.webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body(0x29d83430)
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/webview/webkit2_40+.go:24 +0x39 fp=0x2469f427bcf0 sp=0x2469f427bcb8 pc=0x819139
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver/webview.(*request).Body(0x2469f43cf200)
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/webview/request_linux.go:63 +0x25 fp=0x2469f427bd08 sp=0x2469f427bcf0 pc=0x817de5
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver.(*AssetServer).processWebViewRequestInternal(0x2469f42be140, {0xe64af0, 0x2469f4326918})
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/assetserver_webview.go:98 +0x4ac fp=0x2469f427bf60 sp=0x2469f427bd08 pc=0x83f94c
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver.(*AssetServer).processWebViewRequest(0x2469f42be140, {0xe64af0, 0x2469f4326918})
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/assetserver_webview.go:57 +0x48 fp=0x2469f427bfb8 sp=0x2469f427bf60 pc=0x83f388
github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver.(*AssetServer).ServeWebViewRequest.gowrap1()
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/assetserver_webview.go:49 +0x1f fp=0x2469f427bfe0 sp=0x2469f427bfb8 pc=0x841d7f
runtime.goexit({})
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.27.1.linux-amd64/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x2469f427bfe8 sp=0x2469f427bfe0 pc=0x49b3e1
created by github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/pkg/assetserver.(*AssetServer).ServeWebViewRequest in goroutine 10
	/home/runner/go/pkg/mod/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2@v2.14.0/pkg/assetserver/assetserver_webview.go:49 +0xe5
```

The lines immediately preceding it, in case they matter:

```
(maos-transport-spike:10151): dbind-WARNING **: 06:46:26.915: AT-SPI: Error retrieving accessibility bus address: org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.ServiceUnknown: The name org.a11y.Bus was not provided by any .service files
Overriding existing handler for signal 10. Set JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC if you want WebKit to use a different signal
libEGL warning: DRI3 error: Could not get DRI3 device
libEGL warning: Ensure your X server supports DRI3 to get accelerated rendering
```

The crash reproduced on every run that sent a `FormData` body — the ~2 MiB
upload and the 32-byte one, each in its own process — with the same stack. Runs
of the same binary that sent a 2 MiB `text/plain` body or a 2 MiB
`application/octet-stream` body instead exited 0.

### macOS: the same request arrives with an empty body

No crash; the handler is reached and reports:

```
Content-Type:   multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryQ47DLnq2iyHcBW8V
Content-Length: (header absent)
bytes:          0
parse_error:    NextPart: multipart: NextPart: EOF
```

Identical at 32 bytes and at 2 MiB.

### What does work, on all three platforms

| Body | macOS | Windows | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` + 45-byte `application/json` | ok | ok | ok |
| `POST` + 2 MiB `text/plain` string | ok | ok | ok |
| `POST` + 2 MiB `application/octet-stream` (`Uint8Array`) | ok | ok | ok |
| `POST` + `multipart/form-data`, 32 B | 0 bytes | ok | SIGSEGV |
| `POST` + `multipart/form-data`, 2 MiB | 0 bytes | ok | SIGSEGV |

The 2 MiB binary body arrived byte-for-byte on all three (sha256
`1e075c8d478ad21844e33e830a695ef03a4d2488b69ee275bd8947618bb1be1e`).

One incidental observation while measuring the above: the `Content-Length`
header was empty on every request body on every platform, including bodies that
arrived whole.

### A note on the `webkit2_legacy` fallback

Building without `-tags webkit2_36|40|41` avoids the crash, but that path has no
request-body support at all — `webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body` returns
`http.NoBody` unconditionally:

```go
// pkg/assetserver/webview/webkit2_legacy.go:35
func webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_http_body(_ *C.WebKitURISchemeRequest) io.ReadCloser {
	return http.NoBody
}
```

So on Linux in v2.14.0 the choice appears to be "request bodies work, but a
`FormData` body ends the process" or "request bodies are silently always empty".
Mentioning it in case it's useful for deciding where a fix belongs.

### Workaround we adopted

POST the raw bytes with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and carry the
filename and any metadata in the URL or in request headers. That is measured
working at 2 MiB on all three platforms.

items.title: [v3][macOS] The cross-platform Permissions option is ignored on macOS
items.body:
### Wails version family

v3

### Exact Wails version

v3.0.0-beta.13 (also on `master` @ 9f2fbd3)

### Operating System

macOS

### Description

`WebviewWindowOptions.Permissions` is honoured on Linux (#5552) and on Windows through WebView2 (#5567), but has no effect on macOS. `WebviewWindowDelegate` is the webview's UI delegate and declares `WKUIDelegate` conformance, but never implements `webView:requestMediaCapturePermissionForOrigin:initiatedByFrame:type:decisionHandler:` — so nothing on darwin reads the map.

Capture itself still works. `WKUIDelegate.h` says an unimplemented method behaves as `WKPermissionDecisionPrompt`, so macOS acts as though every window were permanently `PermissionDefault`. What's lost is the other two policies: you can't drop WebKit's prompt for a window that only loads your own content, and you can't deny capture to a window that shouldn't have it.

The docs already describe this as a known limitation — permissions.mdx says the map is "currently ignored on macOS".

### To Reproduce

1. Build a macOS app with `NSCameraUsageDescription` and `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` in its `Info.plist`.
2. Create a window that should refuse capture:
   ```go
   app.Window.NewWithOptions(application.WebviewWindowOptions{
       Permissions: map[application.PermissionType]application.Permission{
           application.PermissionMicrophone: application.PermissionDeny,
           application.PermissionCamera:     application.PermissionDeny,
       },
   })
   ```
3. Call `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({audio: true, video: true})` from it.
4. WebKit prompts, and capture proceeds if the user accepts — the `PermissionDeny` never applies. Configured with `PermissionAllow`, the prompt still appears.

Found by reading the source rather than running it: `git grep requestMediaCapturePermission v3/` comes back empty, and `webview_window_darwin.go:209` is the only `setUIDelegate:`.

### Expected behaviour

The three-way policy the other platforms implement, mapped onto `WKPermissionDecision`:

| `Permission` | macOS decision |
| --- | --- |
| `PermissionDefault` | `WKPermissionDecisionPrompt` — unchanged from today |
| `PermissionAllow` | `WKPermissionDecisionGrant` |
| `PermissionDeny` | `WKPermissionDecisionDeny` |

TCC still gates the device on top, so `PermissionAllow` removes WebKit's prompt but not the system one. Camera and microphone only, matching the current Linux scope — the other three types have no `WKUIDelegate` equivalent.

### Additional context

#6050 implements this.

### System Details

```
Wails CLI      v3.0.0-beta.13
Go             go1.26.2
OS             macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), darwin/arm64, Apple M4 Pro
Xcode          26.6 (17F113), cli tools 2416
CGO_ENABLED    1
```

items.title: [v3] Generated TS bindings throw "Cannot access '$$createTypeN' before initialization" when a generic model is emitted after its holder

milestone.title: v3.0.0 GA
milestone.description: Wails v3.0.0 General Availability. Track relevant v3 work here. Beta releases are nightly builds and are not planned as separate milestones.

items.body:
### Description

`wails3 generate bindings -ts` can emit a models module that throws the moment it is imported:

```
ReferenceError: Cannot access '$$createType1' before initialization
```

This is a runtime crash on first import, not a type error — so it white-screens the app at boot and fails every test suite that touches the bindings, while `tsc` stays perfectly happy.

### Reproduction

Self-contained repro (5 files): https://gist.github.com/hamzabisevac/ce2a1605e949c925ac6293068a08e8d3

Two models are enough. From an empty directory:

```bash
go mod init example.com/tdzrepro
go get github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3@v3.0.0-beta.16
# write main.go (below)
wails3 generate bindings -ts -d out
```

`main.go`:

```go
package main

import "github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3/pkg/application"

// Alpha sorts before Zeta, so the generator emits it first.
type Alpha struct {
	Name string
	Box  Zeta[string]
}

// Zeta is generic; []T and *T each need an element converter.
type Zeta[T any] struct {
	Items []T
	Ref   *T
}

type Service struct{}

func (s *Service) Get() Alpha { return Alpha{} }

func main() {
	app := application.New(application.Options{
		Services: []application.Service{application.NewService(&Service{})},
	})
	_ = app
}
```

The generated `out/example.com/tdzrepro/models.ts` ends with:

```ts
// Private type creation functions
const $$createType0 = Zeta.createFrom($Create.Any);
const $$createType1 = ($$createParamT: any) => $Create.Array($$createParamT);
const $$createType2 = ($$createParamT: any) => $Create.Nullable($$createParamT);
```

To see it throw:

```bash
npm i @wailsio/runtime@3.0.0-beta.16   # package.json with "type": "module"
node --experimental-strip-types -e "import('./out/example.com/tdzrepro/models.ts')"
```

```
ReferenceError: Cannot access '$$createType1' before initialization
```

### Cause

`createFrom` on a generic class resolves its field converters **eagerly**, when it is called, rather than deferring them into the closure it returns:

```ts
static createFrom<T = any>($$createParamT: (source: any) => T): ($$source?: any) => Zeta<T> {
    const $$createField0_0 = $$createType1($$createParamT);   // ← evaluated now
    const $$createField1_0 = $$createType2($$createParamT);   // ← evaluated now
    return ($$source: any = {}) => { /* ... */ };
}
```

`$$createType0` invokes exactly that at module scope. The private-type block is emitted in creation order, so when a holder type is emitted **before** the generic type it instantiates, the eager call receives a lower index than the generic class's own helper arrows — and reads them while they are still in the temporal dead zone.

### The ordering is the whole bug

Rename `Alpha` → `Holder` and `Zeta` → `Box` in `main.go`, change nothing else, and regenerate. The generic type is now emitted first, its helpers land above the eager call, and the identical model graph imports cleanly:

```ts
const $$createType0 = ($$createParamT: any) => $Create.Array($$createParamT);
const $$createType1 = ($$createParamT: any) => $Create.Nullable($$createParamT);
const $$createType2 = Box.createFrom($Create.Any);
```

```
IMPORT OK
```

Same structure, only the names differ. That sensitivity is why this is easy to miss — and why, on a real model graph, it looks like the generator randomly breaks.

### Suggested fixes

Any one of:

1. **Emit the `($$createParamT) => ...` helper arrows ahead of every eager `X.createFrom(...)`** in the private-type block. Smallest change — those arrows close over nothing but `$Create` and their own parameter, so reordering them is semantically inert.
2. Defer field-converter resolution into the closure returned by a generic `createFrom`.
3. Extend the existing lazy-init escape hatch (`$$initCreateTypeN`, `internal/generator/render/create.go`) to generic classes. Today it is applied only to non-class named types, so generic classes take the eager path.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Wails | v3.0.0-beta.16 |
| @wailsio/runtime | 3.0.0-beta.16 |
| Go | go1.26.5 |

items.body:
## Problem

`AutostartManager.EnableWithOptions` accepts a stable `AutostartOptions.Identifier`, but `Disable` discovers registrations by the current executable instead of deleting that identifier. On Windows, a Run value left by an older installation path cannot be removed after the executable moves. The same discovery-based mismatch exists for Linux desktop files and macOS LaunchAgents.

A consumer can work around this by calling `EnableWithOptions` and then `Disable`, but that is not failure-atomic: if enable succeeds and disable fails, a previously disabled app becomes registered at login. Retrying the same sequence cannot reliably restore the disabled state.

## Reproduction

1. Write a Windows Run value under a stable identifier, with the command pointing to an old executable path.
2. Start the application from a new path.
3. Call `AutostartManager.Disable()`.
4. The stable value remains because `windowsAutostart.find()` matches only the current executable.

## Proposed API

Add `DisableWithOptions(AutostartOptions)` (or an equivalent identifier-targeted operation) that validates and removes the exact registration identity used by `EnableWithOptions`. Keep existing `Disable()` behavior for compatibility.

## Acceptance

- Windows removes the exact registry value even when its command points to a moved executable.
- Linux removes the exact `.desktop` filename.
- macOS removes the exact LaunchAgent label while preserving SMAppService cleanup.
- Empty options retain the existing default behavior.
- Invalid identifiers are rejected consistently.
- Native/platform tests cover idempotency and moved executable state.

items.title: [v3/macOS] WKWebView capped at 60 FPS on ProMotion display

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Unscheduled feature work beyond GA. Placement here is not a commitment to a specific release. Goose should move items to a numbered milestone only when that release scope is justified.

items.body:
### Wails version family

v3

### Exact Wails version

v3.0.0-beta.1

### Operating System

macOS

### Description

On a MacBook Pro with a 120 Hz ProMotion display, a Wails v3 WKWebView is capped at approximately 60 FPS even though the same WebKit version is capable of rendering at 120 FPS.

Environment:

- macOS 26.5.2 (Build 25F84)
- MacBook Pro with 120 Hz ProMotion display
- macOS SDK 26.5
- Application binary:
  - minos 12.0
  - sdk 26.5

A simple requestAnimationFrame counter consistently reports approximately 60 FPS inside Wails.

Safari also defaults to approximately 60 FPS, but disabling Safari's "Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps" feature flag immediately allows the same test to run at approximately 120 FPS.

More importantly, applying the equivalent WebKit preference directly to the WKWebView created by Wails also immediately changes the Wails application from approximately 60 FPS to approximately 120 FPS.

The preference is:

PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled

I tested this by modifying v3/pkg/application/webview_window_darwin.go and disabling the preference through the private WKPreferences feature API immediately after the WKWebView is created.

Before:

requestAnimationFrame ≈ 60 FPS

After disabling PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled:

requestAnimationFrame ≈ 120 FPS

This appears particularly interesting on macOS 26 because the related Tauri investigation reports that the 60 FPS cap no longer applies to WKWebView on Tahoe and that this private preference should effectively be a no-op there.

However, with Wails v3 on macOS 26.5.2, the preference clearly still affects rendering cadence: disabling it changes the WebView from 60 Hz to 120 Hz.

Related investigation:

https://github.com/userFRM/tauri-plugin-macos-fps

Their compatibility notes currently state that on macOS 26 Tahoe, WKWebView runs at native refresh rate without the plugin. That does not appear to be the case for the WKWebView created by Wails v3 on my system.

### To Reproduce

1. Run a Wails v3 application on a MacBook Pro with a 120 Hz ProMotion display.

2. Run this code in the frontend:
```
let frames = 0;
let start = performance.now();

function frame(now) {
    frames++;

    if (now - start >= 1000) {
        console.log(
            (frames * 1000 / (now - start)).toFixed(1),
            "FPS"
        );

        frames = 0;
        start = now;
    }

    requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

requestAnimationFrame(frame);
```

3. Observe approximately 60 FPS.

For comparison, in Safari 26 on the same machine:

1. Enable the Develop features.
2. Disable "Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps".
3. Run the same test.
4. Observe approximately 120 FPS.

I then modified Wails' macOS WebView creation code to disable the equivalent private WebKit feature immediately after WKWebView creation.

After rebuilding, the same requestAnimationFrame test reports approximately 120 FPS.

### Expected behaviour

On a 120 Hz ProMotion display, a Wails WKWebView should be capable of receiving rendering updates at the display's native refresh rate rather than being limited to approximately 60 Hz.

Ideally this should work without relying on private WebKit APIs.

I am not necessarily suggesting that Wails should ship the private _features / _setEnabled:forFeature: workaround, since those APIs are undocumented.

The main issue is that Wails' WKWebView appears to remain in WebKit's 60 FPS mode on macOS 26, whereas other investigation suggests that normal WKWebView instances on Tahoe should no longer be capped.

### Screenshots

_No response_

### Attempted Fixes

* Confirmed the MacBook display is running ProMotion.
* Confirmed `requestAnimationFrame` is approximately 60 FPS in Wails.
* Confirmed Safari is initially approximately 60 FPS.
* Disabled Safari's "Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps" feature flag and confirmed Safari immediately reaches approximately 120 FPS.
* Tested loading the Wails frontend over normal `http://localhost` rather than the Wails custom URL scheme. Wails remained at approximately 60 FPS.
* Changed `WKWebViewConfiguration.suppressesIncrementalRendering` from `true` to `false`. No effect; Wails remained approximately 60 FPS.
* Confirmed the application is being built against the macOS 26.5 SDK:

```
cmd LC_BUILD_VERSION
cmdsize 32
platform 1
minos 12.0
sdk 26.5
ntools 1
tool 3
```

* I then modified `v3/pkg/application/webview_window_darwin.go` to disable WebKit's private `PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled` feature on the `WKWebView`.

I added:

```
#import <objc/message.h>

static void disableWebKit60FPSCap(WKWebView *webView) {
    WKPreferences *preferences = webView.configuration.preferences;

    Class preferencesClass = NSClassFromString(@"WKPreferences");
    SEL featuresSelector = NSSelectorFromString(@"_features");
    SEL setEnabledSelector = NSSelectorFromString(@"_setEnabled:forFeature:");

    if (preferencesClass == nil ||
        ![preferencesClass respondsToSelector:featuresSelector] ||
        ![preferences respondsToSelector:setEnabledSelector]) {
        return;
    }

    typedef NSArray *(*FeaturesFn)(id, SEL);
    NSArray *features =
        ((FeaturesFn)objc_msgSend)(preferencesClass, featuresSelector);

    for (id feature in features) {
        NSString *key = [feature valueForKey:@"key"];

        if ([key isEqualToString:@"PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled"]) {
            typedef void (*SetEnabledFn)(id, SEL, BOOL, id);

            ((SetEnabledFn)objc_msgSend)(
                preferences,
                setEnabledSelector,
                NO,
                feature
            );

            return;
        }
    }
}
```

and called it immediately after the `WKWebView` is created:

```objc
WKWebView* webView =
    [[WKWebView alloc] initWithFrame:frame configuration:config];

disableWebKit60FPSCap(webView);
```

After rebuilding, the same `requestAnimationFrame` test changed from approximately 60 FPS to approximately 120 FPS.

Removing this patch and rebuilding immediately brings the rendering FPS back to 60.

So the private WebKit preference workaround is confirmed to affect the Wails WebView on macOS 26.5.2.


### System Details

```shell

# Build Environment

# Dependencies

| *Android NDK            | /Users/nam/Library/Android/sdk/ndk/28.2.13676358           |
| *Android SDK            | /Users/nam/Library/Android/sdk                             |
```

### Additional context

There is an existing investigation/workaround for the same WebKit preference in:

https://github.com/userFRM/tauri-plugin-macos-fps

Its current macOS compatibility documentation reports:

- macOS 13 Ventura: 60 FPS cap exists
- macOS 14 Sonoma: 60 FPS cap exists
- macOS 15 Sequoia: 60 FPS cap exists
- macOS 26 Tahoe: cap removed

It specifically reports testing WKWebView on macOS 26.3.1 with both a 120 Hz ProMotion display and a 165 Hz external display, with both reaching native refresh rate regardless of whether the private preference was changed.

That makes the Wails result unexpected.

On macOS 26.5.2, the Wails v3 WebView remains at approximately 60 FPS, and explicitly disabling PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled still causes it to jump to approximately 120 FPS.

This may indicate some difference in how the Wails WKWebView is configured or instantiated, or some WebKit compatibility behaviour specific to the Wails application.

items.title: [v3, windows]: restore owner activation when closing a foreground modal

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Unscheduled feature work beyond GA. Placement here is not a commitment to a specific release. Goose should move items to a numbered milestone only when that release scope is justified.

items.body:
### Problem

On Windows, closing an attached modal can activate another application's window instead of returning activation to the modal owner. The owner remains visible, but moves behind the unrelated foreground window.

`AttachModal` disables the owner with `EnableWindow(owner, false)`. The current `WM_CLOSE` path re-enables it after `DefWindowProc` has already destroyed the active modal. Re-enabling the owner before destruction is necessary, but is not enough by itself: Windows may still activate the next top-level window in the Alt+Esc order rather than the owner.

### Fix

Before shutting down the modal WebView, record whether the modal is the foreground window. Re-enable its owner before destroying the modal, and if the modal was foreground, call `SetActiveWindow(owner)` first. This keeps the owner active when closing a foreground modal without stealing focus when the modal is already in the background.

This sequence was tested in a downstream Wails application and fixed the foreground/Z-order regression.

items.title: Android binding transport drops CallError cause and custom MarshalError payload

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Unscheduled feature work beyond GA. Placement here is not a commitment to a specific release. Goose should move items to a numbered milestone only when that release scope is justified.

items.body:
### Wails version family

v3

### Exact Wails version

v3.0.0-beta.15

The same transport behaviour is still present on `master` as of 2026-08-29.

### Operating System

Android (experimental), built on macOS arm64 and reproduced on an Android 15 arm64 emulator.

### Description

The Android `JavascriptInterface` binding transport discards the structured `CallError` produced for a bound Go method. In particular, an application's `ServiceOptions.MarshalError` payload is correctly stored in `CallError.Cause`, but Android reduces the wrapped error to `err.Error()` and the JavaScript runtime reconstructs only a plain `Error`.

This makes Android binding semantics differ from the HTTP transport used on other platforms: callers cannot inspect `error.cause`, so structured application errors and session-routing metadata are lost.

The loss occurs in two places:

1. `pkg/application/application_android.go` calls `fail(err.Error())` in `handleRuntimeCallForAndroid`, returning only `{"ok":false,"error":"..."}`.
2. The Android branch of `@wailsio/runtime` rejects with `new Error(envelope.error)`, without restoring `kind`, `message`, or `cause` from a `CallError`.

This is distinct from #5723 / #5858. Those address non-JSON responses in the Android HTTP fallback path and intentionally wrap the error as a string matching the existing `JavascriptInterface` envelope. They do not preserve `CallError.Cause`.

### To Reproduce

Register a service with a custom error marshaler:

```go
type AppError struct {
    State   string `json:"state"`
    Message string `json:"message"`
}

func (e *AppError) Error() string { return e.State + ": " + e.Message }

func marshalError(err error) []byte {
    var appErr *AppError
    if !errors.As(err, &appErr) {
        return nil
    }
    payload, _ := json.Marshal(appErr)
    return payload
}

type Service struct{}

func (*Service) Fail() error {
    return &AppError{State: "login", Message: "Please log in first."}
}

application.NewServiceWithOptions(&Service{}, application.ServiceOptions{
    MarshalError: marshalError,
})
```

Call the generated binding and inspect the rejection:

```js
try {
  await Fail()
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.name)
  console.log(error.message)
  console.log(error.cause)
}
```

On Android, the result is equivalent to:

```text
Error
Binding call failed: Bound method returned an error: login: Please log in first.
undefined
```

The custom structured payload was present in the original `CallError.Cause`, but is no longer available to JavaScript.

### Expected behaviour

Android should preserve the same bound-method error semantics as the standard HTTP transport:

- return the complete `CallError` (`kind`, `message`, and `cause`) in the Android response envelope;
- reconstruct the corresponding JavaScript error, including `error.cause`;
- preserve arbitrary JSON returned by `ServiceOptions.MarshalError`.

For backward compatibility, transport/internal failures could continue accepting a string error, while bound `CallError` values use a structured error object.

### Screenshots

Not applicable.

### Attempted Fixes

- Confirmed that `MarshalError` is invoked and that `bindings.go` assigns its JSON to `CallError.Cause`.
- Confirmed that the Android loss happens after `HandleRuntimeCallWithIDs` returns the wrapped `CallError`.
- Checked current `master`; it still serializes only `err.Error()` and creates a plain JavaScript `Error`.
- Reviewed #5723 and #5858; they fix an adjacent HTTP fallback JSON-parsing problem but do not preserve structured causes.
- Application-side parsing of the final message can recover a textual prefix such as `login`, but cannot recover arbitrary structured fields and is therefore not an equivalent workaround.

### System Details

```shell
Wails CLI      | v3.0.0-beta.15
Go Version     | go1.27.0
Host OS        | macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), arm64, Apple Silicon
Android SDK    | /opt/homebrew/share/android-commandlinetools
Android NDK    | 26.3.11579264
Java           | OpenJDK 21.0.12
Emulator       | Android 15, Google APIs, arm64-v8a
npm            | 11.16.0
```

`wails3 doctor` reports no issues.

### Additional context

A complete fix likely needs both sides of the Android transport to change:

- Go: detect the wrapped `*application.CallError` (for example with `errors.As`) and encode it in the Android envelope instead of calling only `err.Error()`.
- JavaScript runtime: when `envelope.error` is structured, construct `ReferenceError`, `TypeError`, or `RuntimeError` consistently with the HTTP transport and assign its `cause`; continue supporting legacy string envelopes.

Regression coverage should include a bound method using a custom `MarshalError` and assert that an Android runtime rejection exposes the original structured cause.
